\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
\label{sec:discuss_kstar}

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ uniformly across all 8 tested configurations (4 model-mode combinations from Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary} and 4 decoding strategies from the ablation)---establishes that this boundary is not only finite but remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale.

The shallowness of $\Kempirical$ is explained by the rate of information loss across generations.
The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$ across all configurations), reflecting the large distributional gap between human text and first-generation synthetic text.
At the 1v2 boundary, $\auc$ drops by approximately 30 percentage points ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.7039), indicating that the majority of the discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
By the 2v3 boundary, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917---below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose information bottleneck is traversed within two steps.

The feature degradation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides mechanistic evidence for this rapid collapse.
The most discriminative features---surprisal variance (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}) and its derivatives---all capture the heterogeneity of token-level predictability.
Human text exhibits high surprisal variance reflecting diverse syntactic structures and unpredictable discourse patterns.
The first generation step smooths this variance substantially, replacing high-surprisal tokens and atypical constructions with more predictable alternatives; the second step reduces the remaining variance to near-floor levels, leaving insufficient statistical fingerprint for reliable adjacent-depth discrimination.
Crucially, this degradation ordering is consistent across model families (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ for all continuation-mode pairs), suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the autoregressive generation mechanism itself rather than by model-specific biases.

This pattern aligns with findings from the model collapse literature.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations, with minority modes vanishing before the output distribution stabilizes.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination horizon is reached after just two generation steps.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.

The invariance of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$, with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
This robustness suggests that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the fundamental information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.

\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:discuss_transfer}

The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs.
At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 universally, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across generators.

The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.

Two caveats bound this conclusion.
First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (91--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
Second, Qwen-cont$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (91--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.

\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
\label{sec:discuss_features}

While $\Kempirical = 2$ is invariant to decoding strategy (4/4 configurations), the feature importance ordering is not uniformly consistent.
Greedy decoding and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated feature rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with top features dominated by vocabulary diversity measures: \texttt{self\_bleu}, \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, and \texttt{ttr}.
In contrast, greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields a lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction for 6 pairwise comparisons), with $T{=}1.2$ promoting \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to the top ranks.
Notably, \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 under greedy ($\auc = 0.5139$) to rank~5 under $T{=}1.2$ ($\auc = 0.5905$), illustrating how high-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts.

This dissociation reveals an important distinction: the \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} for detecting it depends on the sampling strategy.
High-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts while attenuating vocabulary-diversity signals, shifting which text properties carry the most discriminative power without altering whether adjacent generations can be distinguished.
For practitioners, this implies that a universal depth classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups---surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---to maintain performance across unknown decoding conditions.

The cross-model feature ordering (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides a complementary perspective: among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly consistent (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---dominating uniformly.
A genuine limitation, however, is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens to $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}), indicating that the relative contribution of individual features at the discrimination boundary varies across models even when the aggregate ordering is shared.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:discuss_llm}

Frontier LLMs provide a natural baseline for depth estimation.
On a 500-sample test set with 5 depth classes (depths 0--4), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% accuracy (MAE = 1.15)---both below the OBD-LightGBM baseline of 38.6\% (MAE = 1.11).
Simultaneously, both models achieve approximately 88\% binary accuracy on the human-vs.-synthetic distinction (GPT-5.5: 87.8\%, Claude: 88.2\%).

This gap between binary detection and depth estimation is informative.
Frontier LLMs can reliably determine \emph{whether} a text is machine-generated but cannot estimate \emph{how many generations of recursive processing} it has undergone.
Depth estimation requires sensitivity to subtle distributional shifts between adjacent generations---shifts orders of magnitude smaller than the human-vs.-machine gap.
The 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline, despite its simplicity, captures these fine-grained shifts more effectively than frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting.
This motivates the dedicated feature-engineering approach: the task demands specialized statistical sensitivity rather than general language understanding.
We evaluate only zero-shot prompting; few-shot or chain-of-thought strategies may narrow the gap and warrant future investigation.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

We identify seven limitations that bound the generalizability of our findings.

\emph{Model scale.}
All experiments use models at or below 1.5B parameters (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct).
Larger models may produce higher-fidelity text with weaker depth signatures, potentially shifting $\Kempirical$ beyond~2.

\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
Our recursive generation protocol is a prompt-chain: the same fixed model repeatedly generates from the previous output.
Real-world model collapse involves retrain-chains, where models are retrained on data from earlier generations~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}.
Retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics, potentially producing different $\Kstar$ values.

\emph{Language and domain.}
All experiments use English text from the C4 corpus.
Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.

\emph{Decoding coverage.}
We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
Sensitivity analysis across four decoding configurations shows $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 2$ for $\theta \in [0.60, 0.65]$, and $\Kempirical = 1$ at $\theta = 0.70$ (3 of 4 configurations).
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
On the lower side, Qwen-cont's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
On the upper side, Qwen-rw's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary.
Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.

\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.

\emph{Feature representation.}
The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is unlikely to be optimal.
Learned representations---fine-tuned embeddings or probing classifiers---may capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss, potentially achieving a higher $\Kempirical$.

\subsection{Broader Impact}
\label{sec:broader_impact}

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.

\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.

\paragraph{AI text detection.}
Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.
This additional dimension---how many generations of processing a text has undergone---may prove valuable for provenance tracking and corpus quality assessment, where the binary human/AI label elides important distinctions between lightly and heavily recycled content.

\label{sec:conclusion}

discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ for recursive synthetic text.

continuation and rewrite modes) and 4 decoding strategies---totaling 8
conditions---we establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a universal boundary:

yield 1v2 $\auc$ above $\theta$) confirm statistical significance; the most marginal
case, Qwen-cont, yields a CI lower bound of 0.6015, exceeding $\theta$ by
only 0.15\,pp.

sharp ${\sim}$30\,pp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$: 0.6112--0.7039 across all
conditions), while all 2v3 pairs fall below~$\theta$.

statistical fingerprint is exhausted within two steps.

% === Contribution 2: Ordinal depth estimation framework ===
% Sources: exp_010 (OBD vs baselines), exp_013 (cross-model transfer), exp_005 (feature degradation), exp_011 (LLM zero-shot)
To operationalize depth estimation, we introduced an ordinal binary
decomposition (OBD) framework pairing 15 hand-crafted statistical features
with LightGBM classifiers.
Cross-model transfer experiments demonstrate 80--92\% accuracy retention
across continuation-mode model pairs, with
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieving 91--92\% and 0v1 transfer $\auc$
exceeding 0.96 universally---indicating that depth signals are largely
text-intrinsic rather than generator-specific.
Feature degradation orderings are consistent across architectures
(Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features dominating
uniformly, suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the
autoregressive mechanism itself.
As a reference point, frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus~4.6) achieve
${\sim}$88\% binary human-vs.-synthetic accuracy but only ${\sim}$33\% on
5-class depth estimation, below OBD-LightGBM's 38.6\%---confirming that
fine-grained depth discrimination requires specialized statistical features
rather than general language understanding.

% === Contribution 3: Graduated filtering (C3) ===
% Source: exp_006 (RUNNING — results pending)
The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary implies a natural trichotomy---human (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$)---that can be exploited for depth-aware data curation.

% 与 binary filtering 和 no-filter baseline 的对比。

% === Limitations + Future Work ===

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-cont 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
\label{tab:kstar_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]
1v2 & 0.6955 & 0.6539 & 0.6145 & 0.6112 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.6859,\,.7041]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6454,\,.6630]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6045,\,.6247]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6015,\,.6213]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
2v3 & 0.5893 & 0.5514 & 0.5496 & 0.5609 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.5795,\,.5991]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5417,\,.5628]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5399,\,.5596]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5511,\,.5712]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
3v4 & 0.5435 & 0.5152 & 0.5091 & 0.5409 \\
4v5 & 0.5340 & 0.5136 & 0.5045 & 0.5141 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rw ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-cont (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rw ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-cont (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models studied.

The most marginal case is Qwen-cont, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
boundary closer to the detection threshold.

The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
Qwen-rw (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-cont (0.6112).
Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
(Qwen-rw vs.\ Qwen-cont: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
across models in the same mode
(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
of detectability than model identity.
We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
rapidly.

\label{sec:generation_mode}

0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.

and narrows at 3v4
(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),

with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.

whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rw trained,
Qwen-cont tested---retains 82\%
(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
available in rewrite-mode data
(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.

This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
continuation-mode model.

transfer poorly across models
(Qwen-rw$\to$Pythia/OLMo: 61--63\% retention).
Continuation-mode classifiers sacrifice 8.4\,pp of within-model
$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\centering
\small

and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,

and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.

  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line). \label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rw ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),

3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
\label{tab:kstar_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]
1v2 & 0.6955 & 0.6539 & 0.6145 & 0.6112 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.6859,\,.7041]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6454,\,.6630]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6045,\,.6247]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6015,\,.6213]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
2v3 & 0.5893 & 0.5514 & 0.5496 & 0.5609 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.5795,\,.5991]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5417,\,.5628]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5399,\,.5596]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5511,\,.5712]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
3v4 & 0.5435 & 0.5152 & 0.5091 & 0.5409 \\
4v5 & 0.5340 & 0.5136 & 0.5045 & 0.5141 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models studied.

The most marginal case is Qwen-cont, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
boundary closer to the detection threshold.

The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
Qwen-rw (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-cont (0.6112).
Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
(Qwen-rw vs.\ Qwen-cont: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
across models in the same mode
(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
of detectability than model identity.
We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
rapidly.
OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
random for this model.
Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
while Qwen-cont shows weak but detectable discrimination through
3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
classification.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
model.}
\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
Qwen-rw
  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\
Pythia
  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\
OLMo
  & 0.2768 & 0.3450 & \textbf{0.3822} & 0.3244 \\
Qwen-cont
  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
Rows: training model; columns: test model.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).
Diagonal entries are within-model baselines.}
\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
\end{figure}

Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
predictions is largely preserved.
Qwen-cont$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
(84--85\% accuracy retention),
and Qwen-cont$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.

Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
(45--50\% by $\tau$).
The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rw retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
to Qwen-cont, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.

At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
distinction is universally transferable regardless of generator
or mode.
The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.

The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
further.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
\label{sec:feature_degradation}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
independently for each model and comparing them via rank
correlation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
model configuration.
Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.
Spearman $\rho$ (continuation-mode pairs): Pythia--OLMo 0.95,
Pythia--Qwen-cont 0.9143, OLMo--Qwen-cont 0.85.}
\label{tab:top_features}
\begin{tabular}{cllll}
\toprule
Rank & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-rw & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
1
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \texttt{freq\_entropy}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}} \\
2
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}} \\
3
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings
are highly correlated:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\rho = 0.95$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-cont $\rho = 0.9143$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-cont $\rho = 0.85$
(all $\rho \geq 0.85$).
The top-3 features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std},
and \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---are shared (up to ordering) across
all three continuation-mode configurations
(Table~\ref{tab:top_features}).
All three measure variability of surprisal or its derivatives,
capturing the \emph{heterogeneity} of token-level predictability
across the text.
That these features degrade in a shared order across generators
suggests a common mechanism: each generation step smooths the
token-level surprisal landscape, reducing its variance in a
model-independent fashion.

Qwen-rewrite diverges: its top-ranked feature is
\texttt{freq\_entropy}, a lexical diversity measure absent from
the continuation-mode top-3 for any model.
This corroborates the transfer results in
Section~\ref{sec:transfer}---rewrite-mode classifiers learn
partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the
shared surprisal-based signals.

Kendall $\tau$ provides a complementary, more conservative
perspective:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\tau = 0.733$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-cont $\tau = 0.695$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-cont $\tau = 0.543$.
Cross-mode correlations are lower:
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-rw $\tau = 0.467$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-rw $\tau = 0.429$.

\paragraph{Limitation.}
The high Spearman $\rho$ characterizes the \emph{aggregate}
feature ranking, but at the depth-pair level the agreement
weakens: $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary.
This means that while the overall importance ordering is shared,
the relative contribution of individual features at the
discrimination boundary---where precision matters most---varies
across models.
We view this as a genuine limitation of the text-intrinsic
interpretation and a direction for future investigation.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Generation Mode Effect}
\label{sec:generation_mode}

Finally, we ask whether generation mode---an experimental design choice rather than a text property---affects depth detectability.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct provides a controlled comparison: rewrite (instruction-based paraphrasing) and continuation (prompt truncation) share the same model weights, as defined in Section~\ref{sec:method}, isolating the effect of generation protocol.

Rewrite mode yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ than continuation:
0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.
The advantage persists at 2v3
(0.5893 vs.\ 0.5609, $\Delta = +$2.8\,pp)
and narrows at 3v4
(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),
with both modes converging toward chance at deeper levels.
The amplified detectability under rewrite mode is consistent
with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.

Transfer between modes is asymmetric.
A classifier trained on Qwen-cont and evaluated on Qwen-rw
retains 89\% of within-model accuracy
(0.3440 vs.\ 0.3875 diagonal),
whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rw trained,
Qwen-cont tested---retains 82\%
(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
available in rewrite-mode data
(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.

This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
continuation-mode model.
Qwen-cont's top feature (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}) is shared
with Pythia and OLMo, confirming that continuation mode
captures primarily text-intrinsic depth signals.

The practical implication is a detectability--generalizability
tradeoff.
Rewrite-mode classifiers achieve higher absolute $\auc$ but
transfer poorly across models
(Qwen-rw$\to$Pythia/OLMo: 61--63\% retention).
Continuation-mode classifiers sacrifice 8.4\,pp of within-model
$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer
(Qwen-cont$\to$Pythia: 84--85\%).
For deployment scenarios requiring model-agnostic depth
estimation, continuation-mode features provide a more reliable
foundation despite lower raw discriminability.

\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each

1

\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

\end{table}

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models studied.

The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound

of detectability than model identity.

and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

random for this model.
Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),

3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
classification.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
model.}
\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
Qwen-rw
  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\

  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\

  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\

\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}

Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
predictions is largely preserved.
Qwen-cont$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
(84--85\% accuracy retention),
and Qwen-cont$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.

Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
(45--50\% by $\tau$).
The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rw retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
to Qwen-cont, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.

At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
distinction is universally transferable regardless of generator
or mode.
The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.

The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
further.

\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
\label{sec:feature_degradation}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
independently for each model and comparing them via rank
correlation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
model configuration.
Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.

Pythia--Qwen-cont 0.9143, OLMo--Qwen-cont 0.85.}
\label{tab:top_features}

\toprule
Rank & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-rw & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
1
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \texttt{freq\_entropy}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}} \\
2
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}} \\
3
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings
are highly correlated:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\rho = 0.95$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-cont $\rho = 0.9143$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-cont $\rho = 0.85$
(all $\rho \geq 0.85$).
The top-3 features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std},
and \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---are shared (up to ordering) across
all three continuation-mode configurations
(Table~\ref{tab:top_features}).
All three measure variability of surprisal or its derivatives,
capturing the \emph{heterogeneity} of token-level predictability
across the text.
That these features degrade in a shared order across generators
suggests a common mechanism: each generation step smooths the
token-level surprisal landscape, reducing its variance in a
model-independent fashion.

Qwen-rewrite diverges: its top-ranked feature is
\texttt{freq\_entropy}, a lexical diversity measure absent from
the continuation-mode top-3 for any model.
This corroborates the transfer results in
Section~\ref{sec:transfer}---rewrite-mode classifiers learn
partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the
shared surprisal-based signals.

Kendall $\tau$ provides a complementary, more conservative
perspective:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\tau = 0.733$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-cont $\tau = 0.695$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-cont $\tau = 0.543$.
Cross-mode correlations are lower:
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-rw $\tau = 0.467$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-rw $\tau = 0.429$.

The high Spearman $\rho$ characterizes the \emph{aggregate}
feature ranking, but at the depth-pair level the agreement
weakens: $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary.
This means that while the overall importance ordering is shared,
the relative contribution of individual features at the
discrimination boundary---where precision matters most---varies
across models.
We view this as a genuine limitation of the text-intrinsic
interpretation and a direction for future investigation.

\subsection{Generation Mode Effect}
\label{sec:generation_mode}

Finally, we ask whether generation mode---an experimental design choice rather than a text property---affects depth detectability.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct provides a controlled comparison: rewrite (instruction-based paraphrasing) and continuation (prompt truncation) share the same model weights, as defined in Section~\ref{sec:method}, isolating the effect of generation protocol.

Rewrite mode yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ than continuation:
0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.
The advantage persists at 2v3
(0.5893 vs.\ 0.5609, $\Delta = +$2.8\,pp)
and narrows at 3v4
(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),
with both modes converging toward chance at deeper levels.
The amplified detectability under rewrite mode is consistent
with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.

Transfer between modes is asymmetric.
A classifier trained on Qwen-cont and evaluated on Qwen-rw
retains 89\% of within-model accuracy
(0.3440 vs.\ 0.3875 diagonal),
whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rw trained,
Qwen-cont tested---retains 82\%
(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
available in rewrite-mode data
(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.

This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
continuation-mode model.
Qwen-cont's top feature (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}) is shared
with Pythia and OLMo, confirming that continuation mode
captures primarily text-intrinsic depth signals.

The practical implication is a detectability--generalizability
tradeoff.
Rewrite-mode classifiers achieve higher absolute $\auc$ but
transfer poorly across models
(Qwen-rw$\to$Pythia/OLMo: 61--63\% retention).
Continuation-mode classifiers sacrifice 8.4\,pp of within-model
$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer
(Qwen-cont$\to$Pythia: 84--85\%).
For deployment scenarios requiring model-agnostic depth
estimation, continuation-mode features provide a more reliable
foundation despite lower raw discriminability.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
\label{tab:kstar_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]
1v2 & 0.6955 & 0.6539 & 0.6145 & 0.6112 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.6859,\,.7041]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6454,\,.6630]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6045,\,.6247]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6015,\,.6213]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
2v3 & 0.5893 & 0.5514 & 0.5496 & 0.5609 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.5795,\,.5991]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5417,\,.5628]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5399,\,.5596]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5511,\,.5712]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
3v4 & 0.5435 & 0.5152 & 0.5091 & 0.5409 \\
4v5 & 0.5340 & 0.5136 & 0.5045 & 0.5141 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models studied.

The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
boundary closer to the detection threshold.

The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
across models in the same mode
(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
of detectability than model identity.
We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
rapidly.
OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
random for this model.
Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
classification.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
model.}
\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
Qwen-rw
  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\
Pythia
  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\
OLMo
  & 0.2768 & 0.3450 & \textbf{0.3822} & 0.3244 \\
Qwen-cont
  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
Rows: training model; columns: test model.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).
Diagonal entries are within-model baselines.}
\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
\end{figure}

Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
predictions is largely preserved.
Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
(84--85\% accuracy retention),
and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.

Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
(45--50\% by $\tau$).
The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.

At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
distinction is universally transferable regardless of generator
or mode.
The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.

The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
further.

\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
\label{sec:feature_degradation}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
independently for each model and comparing them via rank
correlation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each

partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the

perspective:

\centering
\small

\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each

whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rw trained,
Qwen-cont tested---retains 82\%

available in rewrite-mode data
(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),

rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================

\centering
\small

and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.

  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]

\end{table}

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:

followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed). \label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
\label{tab:kstar_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]
1v2 & 0.6955 & 0.6539 & 0.6145 & 0.6112 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.6859,\,.7041]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6454,\,.6630]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6045,\,.6247]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6015,\,.6213]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
2v3 & 0.5893 & 0.5514 & 0.5496 & 0.5609 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.5795,\,.5991]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5417,\,.5628]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5399,\,.5596]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5511,\,.5712]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
3v4 & 0.5435 & 0.5152 & 0.5091 & 0.5409 \\
4v5 & 0.5340 & 0.5136 & 0.5045 & 0.5141 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models studied.

The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
boundary closer to the detection threshold.

The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
across models in the same mode
(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
of detectability than model identity.
We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
rapidly.
OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
random for this model.
Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
classification.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
model.}
\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
Qwen-rw
  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\
Pythia
  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\
OLMo
  & 0.2768 & 0.3450 & \textbf{0.3822} & 0.3244 \\
Qwen-cont
  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
Rows: training model; columns: test model.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).
Diagonal entries are within-model baselines.}
\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
\end{figure}

Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
predictions is largely preserved.
Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
(84--85\% accuracy retention),
and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.

Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
(45--50\% by $\tau$).
The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.

At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
distinction is universally transferable regardless of generator
or mode.
The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.

The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
further.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
\label{sec:feature_degradation}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
independently for each model and comparing them via rank
correlation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
model configuration.
Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.
Spearman $\rho$ (continuation-mode pairs): Pythia--OLMo 0.95,
Pythia--Qwen-continuation 0.9143, OLMo--Qwen-continuation 0.85.}
\label{tab:top_features}
\begin{tabular}{cllll}
\toprule
Rank & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-rw & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
1
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \texttt{freq\_entropy}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}} \\
2
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}} \\
3
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings
are highly correlated:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\rho = 0.95$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.9143$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.85$
(all $\rho \geq 0.85$).
The top-3 features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std},
and \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---are shared (up to ordering) across
all three continuation-mode configurations
(Table~\ref{tab:top_features}).
All three measure variability of surprisal or its derivatives,
capturing the \emph{heterogeneity} of token-level predictability
across the text.
That these features degrade in a shared order across generators
suggests a common mechanism: each generation step smooths the
token-level surprisal landscape, reducing its variance in a
model-independent fashion.

Qwen-rewrite diverges: its top-ranked feature is
\texttt{freq\_entropy}, a lexical diversity measure absent from
the continuation-mode top-3 for any model.
This corroborates the transfer results in
Section~\ref{sec:transfer}---rewrite-mode classifiers learn
partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the
shared surprisal-based signals.

Kendall $\tau$ provides a complementary, more conservative
perspective:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\tau = 0.733$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.695$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.543$.
Cross-mode correlations are lower:
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.467$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.429$.

\paragraph{Limitation.}
The high Spearman $\rho$ characterizes the \emph{aggregate}
feature ranking, but at the depth-pair level the agreement
weakens: $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary.
This means that while the overall importance ordering is shared,
the relative contribution of individual features at the
discrimination boundary---where precision matters most---varies
across models.
We view this as a genuine limitation of the text-intrinsic
interpretation and a direction for future investigation.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Generation Mode Effect}
\label{sec:generation_mode}

Finally, we ask whether generation mode---an experimental design choice rather than a text property---affects depth detectability.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct provides a controlled comparison: rewrite (instruction-based paraphrasing) and continuation (prompt truncation) share the same model weights, as defined in Section~\ref{sec:method}, isolating the effect of generation protocol.

Rewrite mode yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ than continuation:
0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.
The advantage persists at 2v3
(0.5893 vs.\ 0.5609, $\Delta = +$2.8\,pp)
and narrows at 3v4
(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),
with both modes converging toward chance at deeper levels.
The amplified detectability under rewrite mode is consistent
with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.

Transfer between modes is asymmetric.
A classifier trained on Qwen-cont and evaluated on Qwen-rw
retains 89\% of within-model accuracy
(0.3440 vs.\ 0.3875 diagonal),
whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rw trained,
Qwen-cont tested---retains 82\%
(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
available in rewrite-mode data
(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.

This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
continuation-mode model.
Qwen-cont's top feature (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}) is shared
with Pythia and OLMo, confirming that continuation mode
captures primarily text-intrinsic depth signals.

The practical implication is a detectability--generalizability
tradeoff.
Rewrite-mode classifiers achieve higher absolute $\auc$ but
transfer poorly across models
(Qwen-rw$\to$Pythia/OLMo: 61--63\% retention).
Continuation-mode classifiers sacrifice 8.4\,pp of within-model
$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer
(Qwen-cont$\to$Pythia: 84--85\%).
For deployment scenarios requiring model-agnostic depth
estimation, continuation-mode features provide a more reliable
foundation despite lower raw discriminability.

mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among

further.

\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.

independently for each model and comparing them via rank
correlation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
model configuration.
Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.
Spearman $\rho$ (continuation-mode pairs): Pythia--OLMo 0.95,
Pythia--Qwen-continuation 0.9143, OLMo--Qwen-continuation 0.85.}
\label{tab:top_features}
\begin{tabular}{cllll}
\toprule
Rank & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-rw & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
1
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \texttt{freq\_entropy}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}} \\
2
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}} \\
3
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
